summary: Defines a URL scheme for pointing to objects on an IMAP server, such as mailboxes or messages. It obsoletes RFC 2192 and updates RFC 4467. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: An IMAP URL identifies a mail server and can point to a mailbox, search result, message, or message part. Some URLs can also carry an authorization token that limits access to the referenced content.

subtitle: A URL format for referring to IMAP servers, mailboxes, messages, and message parts.

tldr.problem: IMAP provides access to remote mail stores, but applications need a standard way to refer to a server, mailbox, search result, message, or part of a message.
tldr.mechanism: The imap: URL scheme can include a server, optional user and authentication information, mailbox, search, message UID, section, byte range, and an optional URLAUTH authorization token.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5092 obsoletes RFC 2192 and updates RFC 4467. Clients must treat credentials in URLs carefully because the named server may not be trusted.

today: RFC 5092 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2192 and updates RFC 4467. It is itself updated by RFC 5593.

sections.title: The IMAP URL Forms
sections.content:
The imap: URL scheme identifies IMAP servers, mailboxes, messages, message parts, and searches. The server can be followed by a mailbox name, an optional search, or a message UID and optional part or byte range.

If the URL omits the port, it defaults to 143. The formal syntax in the RFC's ABNF section is authoritative when it differs from the explanatory forms.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMAP URL can identify a server, a mailbox, search results, or a specific message part. The URL's path and parameters say which item the client should access.

sections.title: User Names and Authentication
sections.content:
The optional user name identifies a mailbox naming scope and may be used for authentication. If neither a user name nor a mechanism is supplied, a client MUST authenticate anonymously. An ;AUTH= parameter can name an authentication mechanism, while ;AUTH=* asks the client to choose one.

Because URLs can come from untrusted sources, clients must avoid sending credentials to an untrusted server. The RFC lists trusted URLs, site policy, user confirmation, server validation, or mechanisms that reveal no reusable credentials as safeguards.
sections.plainLanguage: A URL can specify a user and an authentication method. If it does not, the client uses anonymous access; if credentials are needed, the client must check that the server is trusted.

sections.title: Mailboxes, Searches, and Messages
sections.content:
A mailbox URL can include UIDVALIDITY to show which version of the mailbox it refers to. A search component supplies arguments for the IMAP SEARCH command. A message URL uses a UID and can select a MIME section and byte range.

Characters that are unsafe or reserved in a URL, such as spaces, semicolons, or question marks, MUST be percent-encoded. If a UIDVALIDITY value no longer matches the mailbox, the URL is treated as stale.
sections.plainLanguage: The URL can narrow a mailbox reference to search results or a particular message and part. Percent-encoding keeps special characters from being confused with URL separators.

sections.title: URLAUTH Links and Access Limits
sections.content:
On servers that advertise URLAUTH, a message URL can carry an access identifier, authorization mechanism, and token. The token is generated using the URL and a per-user, per-mailbox access key with at least 128 bits of entropy.

An optional EXPIRE value sets the latest time when the URL is valid. Access identifiers can limit use to a submitting user, a particular user, any authenticated user, or any session. The token must be at least 32 hexadecimal digits and URLAUTH appears at the end of the URL.
sections.plainLanguage: A URLAUTH link carries a token that authorizes access to specified message content. Its access identifier can restrict who may use it, and an expiration time can limit how long it works.

sections.title: Relative URLs and Mailbox Names
sections.content:
Relative IMAP URLs follow the generic URI resolution rules. The authentication mechanism is inherited from a base URL unless the reference names a different user and server. Implementations MUST NOT generate or accept relative-path IMAP references.

Mailbox names use slash-based URL paths only when slash is also the mailbox hierarchy delimiter. IMAP modified UTF-7 mailbox names MUST be converted to UTF-8 and then percent-encoded for URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: A relative IMAP URL can reuse the server and authentication details of a base URL. Mailbox names with non-ASCII characters are converted to UTF-8 and percent-encoded.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A URL may name an untrusted server, and sending a password there can compromise an account. A client must not use a stored plaintext password without the user's explicit permission to send it to that host.

Clients seeking confidentiality or integrity SHOULD use STARTTLS before authentication or a SASL mechanism that provides a confidentiality layer. URLAUTH identifiers for authuser or anonymous should be used only for content intended for those audiences.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMAP URL can direct a client to a server controlled by someone else. The client should verify the destination and protect credentials before authenticating.
